articles.headline: La N-547 entre Melide y Arzúa suma otro accidente grave en menos de una semana
articles.subtitle: El siniestro, ocurrido este fin de semana, es el segundo de consideración en ese tramo en siete días y reactiva las críticas por el retraso de la A-54, que debería haber vaciado de tráfico la carretera vieja.
articles.body:
La carretera N-547, entre Melide y Arzúa, ha sumado un nuevo accidente de consideración, el segundo en menos de una semana en ese mismo tramo. El siniestro vuelve a poner el foco sobre una vía que sigue soportando el tráfico que la autovía A-54 debería haber absorbido hace años.

El tramo Palas de Rei–Melide de la A-54 ya está en servicio, pero el enlace hasta Arzúa continúa pendiente, de modo que buena parte de los vehículos que cruzan la comarca siguen circulando por la carretera convencional. Los alcaldes de la zona llevan meses reclamando un calendario firme para los tramos que faltan.

El Concello de Arzúa ha insistido por escrito en que los retrasos de la autovía se traducen directamente en más tráfico y más riesgo sobre la N-547, y ha pedido que se concrete cuándo quedará cerrada la conexión con Santiago. Por ahora, la única referencia oficial es la relación de tramos ya entregados por el Ministerio de Transportes.

sources.name: Ministerio de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible

articles.headline: Lugo estrena jaulas trampa contra los jabalíes en pleno casco urbano tras capturar 14 en una semana
articles.subtitle: La Xunta autorizó instalar recintos de captura en el entorno del ayuntamiento y las cifras de los primeros días confirman la sobrepoblación de una especie que ya campea por calles y jardines.
articles.body:
El Ayuntamiento de Lugo y la Xunta han empezado a capturar jabalíes con jaulas trampa instaladas en pleno entorno urbano, una medida que hasta ahora se reservaba al medio rural. La Consellería destaca que los recintos colocados en la ciudad capturaron catorce ejemplares en su primera semana de funcionamiento.

La decisión responde a la sobrepoblación de una especie que ya se deja ver en jardines, rotondas y calles del extrarradio. La Xunta autorizó la instalación de los cercados en las inmediaciones del consistorio y ha defendido su eficacia frente a otros métodos de control.

El sistema no está exento de críticas. Parte de los vecinos y de los colectivos animalistas cuestionan el uso de jaulas en zonas habitadas, mientras el sector agrario reclama que los dispositivos se extiendan también a las parroquias del rural, donde los daños en cultivos y maizales se han disparado en los últimos años.

articles.headline: Miriam González lanza Democracia21 para concurrir al 29-N y promete bajar impuestos de vivienda a los menores de 35
articles.subtitle: La abogada presenta en Madrid y Barcelona un partido centrista que pretende pescar en el electorado desencantado con los bloques y coloca la fiscalidad de la vivienda en el centro de su oferta.
articles.body:
La abogada Miriam González ha presentado Democracia21, la formación con la que pretende concurrir a las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. El partido se estrena en Madrid y Barcelona y llega a la precampaña con una oferta centrada en la vivienda y en la fiscalidad de los jóvenes.

Entre sus primeras propuestas está una rebaja de impuestos ligada a la compra de vivienda para los menores de 35 años, un guiño directo a un grupo de edad que las encuestas sitúan entre los más castigados por el precio del alquiler y de la hipoteca.

Democracia21 se presenta como una alternativa de centro ajena a los bloques que se disputan el 29-N, y busca captar votantes que, según sus promotores, no se reconocen ni en el PP y Vox ni en el PSOE y sus socios. El proyecto arranca sin representación institucional y con la dificultad añadida de concurrir a unos comicios convocados con muy poco margen.

articles.headline: Sánchez promete reforzar el decreto de vivienda y acusa a PP y Vox de difundir «bulos» sobre el voto por correo
articles.subtitle: El presidente despliega un plan de ayudas pensado para jóvenes y mujeres, reivindica su figura ante las urnas del 29-N y sostiene que la derecha siembra dudas sobre el voto postal porque teme perder.
articles.body:
Pedro Sánchez ha prometido reforzar por decreto las medidas de vivienda aprobadas por el Gobierno y ha acusado a PP y Vox de lanzar «bulos» sobre el voto por correo de cara al 29-N. En sus intervenciones de campaña ha sostenido que quienes cuestionan el voto postal lo hacen porque «tienen miedo a perder».

El Ejecutivo prepara un plan millonario de ayudas directas que alcanzaría a cerca de la mitad del electorado, con especial atención a los jóvenes y a las mujeres, según la reconstrucción que hace la prensa de las medidas anunciadas en precampaña.

Sánchez ha vuelto a los escenarios donde su partido se siente más cómodo, con un discurso de confrontación con la derecha y apelaciones a la movilización. Las encuestas publicadas esta semana mantienen una mayoría holgada de PP y Vox, mientras el PSOE absorbe voto de la izquierda situada a su izquierda.

articles.headline: Juan Carlos I renuncia a demandar a Corinna Larsen y a recuperar los 65 millones que le donó
articles.subtitle: El rey emérito descarta la demanda por honor y fraude que sus abogados preparaban desde abril de 2025, después de que La Zarzuela y su propio entorno le aconsejaran no volver a los tribunales.
articles.body:
Juan Carlos I ha renunciado a emprender acciones judiciales contra Corinna Larsen y contra el abogado suizo Dante Canónica, director de la fundación panameña Lucum, y con ello desiste de recuperar los 65 millones de euros que entregó a la empresaria. La demanda, anunciada en abril de 2025 por delitos contra el honor y fraude, nunca llegó a presentarse.

Sus abogados manejaban reclamar unos 70 millones a Larsen y 3,5 millones a Canónica, sosteniendo que el rey emérito se sintió engañado por ambos. El anuncio de aquella batalla judicial causó malestar en La Zarzuela, y personas de su círculo íntimo le aconsejaron que desistiera.

El dinero procedía de 100 millones de dólares que el entonces jefe del Estado recibió en 2008 del Ministerio de Finanzas de Arabia Saudí durante el reinado de Abdalá bin Abdulaziz, ocultos después en la fundación panameña. Con esta decisión, el emérito cierra la vía civil para intentar recuperar un patrimonio que siempre estuvo depositado fuera de España, entre Suiza y Panamá.

articles.headline: El Gobierno descarta intervenir los precios del alquiler mientras la acampada de la Puerta del Sol cumple dos semanas
articles.subtitle: Economía defiende ante Bruselas no topar las rentas mientras Calviño sostuvo lo contrario dentro del Consejo de Ministros, y la protesta por la vivienda encadena otra semana sin señales de retirada.
articles.body:
El Ministerio de Economía ha defendido ante la Comisión Europea su negativa a intervenir los precios del alquiler, una posición que contrasta con lo que la vicepresidenta Calviño sostuvo dentro del Consejo de Ministros, según la reconstrucción de los hechos que publica la prensa a partir de los documentos remitidos a Bruselas.

Ese doble mensaje llega en plena precampaña y con la vivienda instalada como el asunto que más preocupa a los votantes. Un sondeo publicado este domingo refleja un empate técnico entre quienes respaldan los decretos del Gobierno y quienes los rechazan, una división que ninguna de las partes ha logrado romper.

En la calle, la acampada de la Puerta del Sol cumple ya dos semanas. Los convocantes mantienen la protesta y reclaman medidas sobre el parque público de alquiler, mientras el Ejecutivo insiste en que su decreto, ya en vigor, es la respuesta posible dentro del marco legal vigente.

articles.headline: UUP picks ex-Tory defector Matthew Robinson for East Londonderry
articles.subtitle: The Ulster Unionists have chosen a Portstewart man who left the Conservatives this year, betting that his policy background can win back a constituency that was once unionist heartland.
articles.body:
The Ulster Unionist Party has selected Matthew Robinson as its candidate for East Londonderry at next May's Assembly election. Robinson, 38, lives in Portstewart and defected from the Conservatives earlier this year, having previously stood for them in North Down and appeared regularly on broadcast media defending the last UK government.

He told the News Letter that unionism needed new leadership after two decades he said had not delivered on Northern Ireland's potential, describing the movement's politics as too often stale, tribal and negative. He is backing the direction set by the UUP's Jon Burrows.

Robinson said he would focus on economic growth, farming, education and health services across the north coast constituency, framing his pitch around younger voters who might otherwise leave. His selection follows the party's recruitment of defected DUP councillor Dr Kathryn Owen to stand in South Belfast, part of a wider pattern of the UUP recruiting candidates from rival parties.

The UUP has not held East Londonderry for several assembly terms, and the seat is one of a handful where the party is trying to rebuild support after a run of poor results.

articles.headline: Trump tells Ukraine it needs a 'new president' as Kyiv strikes a Russian oil terminal
articles.subtitle: The US president said it was time for new leadership in Kyiv after Volodymyr Zelensky condemned his diesel deal with Vladimir Putin, while Russian glide bombs killed at least 20 people in Zaporizhzhia.
articles.body:
Donald Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to have a new president, hours after Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the US deal to buy Russian diesel as a gift to Moscow. Speaking on Saturday, Trump attacked the Ukrainian leader directly, and the BBC reported that the remarks were prompted by Zelensky's criticism of the arrangement struck with Vladimir Putin.

Ukraine answered on the battlefield rather than in words, hitting a large Russian oil terminal in an attack Kyiv framed as a response to the diesel agreement. Russia replied with a glide-bomb raid on Zaporizhzhia that killed at least 20 people.

The exchange marks the sharpest rupture yet between Washington and Kyiv since the deal was announced. Analysts quoted by the BBC said the diesel purchase shows how hard the pressure on fuel prices has become for the US administration, and Ukrainian officials now face the prospect of negotiating aid and weapons with a White House that is openly questioning their leadership.

articles.headline: Twelve killed as Houthi attack hits a Riyadh airport for a third time this week
articles.subtitle: Saudi authorities say more than 300 people were hurt at King Khalid airport; the Houthis claim the strike, governments worldwide condemn it, and Donald Trump says he may join Saudi retaliation.
articles.body:
At least 12 people were killed and more than 300 injured when an attack hit Riyadh's King Khalid international airport, according to Saudi authorities. It is the third strike on Saudi airport infrastructure this week and by far the deadliest, with Yemen's Houthis claiming responsibility.

The attack drew condemnation from governments across the region and beyond. Riyadh has said it will respond, and Yemeni government forces allied against the Houthis reported advances near Taiz and the Bab al-Mandab strait as the fighting widened along several fronts.

Donald Trump said the United States was weighing whether to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, telling reporters a decision would be taken shortly, and said he would speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Washington had already been drawn into a parallel confrontation with Iran over shipping in the Gulf, and the airport attack has sharpened the argument inside the administration for a wider response.

articles.headline: US forces disable a ship trying to run the Iran blockade in the Gulf of Oman
articles.subtitle: The commercial vessel had left an Iranian port; separately, a supertanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine on a route Iran's authorities had not authorised.
articles.body:
American forces have disabled a commercial ship that was attempting to run the blockade on Iran in the Gulf of Oman, according to Al Jazeera. The vessel had departed from an Iranian port, and the episode is the latest in a series of incidents that have turned the shipping lanes off Iran's coast into some of the most dangerous water in the world.

In a separate case, a supertanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after striking a mine while travelling along a route that Iranian authorities had not authorised, Spanish media reported. The combined effect has pushed insurance costs and freight rates on the route sharply higher.

Roughly a fifth of the world's oil moves through Hormuz, and the escalation has revived the argument over Europe's dependence on fossil fuels. As one Spanish analysis put it, the second energy crisis in five years has done more than any climate summit to undermine resistance to the green transition.

articles.headline: Gaza's ceasefire reaches one year with almost 1,500 dead and protests worldwide
articles.subtitle: A year after the truce meant to end the war, strikes have continued and the toll has kept climbing, drawing pro-Palestinian marches from London to cities across Europe and beyond.
articles.body:
A year after the ceasefire that was supposed to end the war in Gaza, the truce has held in name only. El País reports that almost 1,500 people have been killed since it came into force, and Israeli strikes have continued, including an attack that destroyed a building in the territory in recent days.

The anniversary brought demonstrators onto the streets from London to cities across Europe and beyond, with marchers calling for a durable end to the campaign and for accountability. In the British capital, thousands gathered to express support for Palestinians, marking what organisers describe as a third year of genocide.

Regional diplomacy remains stalled. The same week saw world governments condemn a Houthi attack on Riyadh's airport and Washington weigh joining Saudi retaliation in Yemen, underlining how far the conflicts of the region have become entangled with one another.

articles.headline: Gunman kills eight in a Pennsylvania house and then turns the weapon on himself
articles.subtitle: Reports differ on the toll, with some outlets saying nine died, among them two children and a pregnant woman; police say the shooter opened fire inside a home before killing himself.
articles.body:
A man opened fire inside a house in Pennsylvania, killing members of the household before taking his own life, according to accounts reported by Spanish media. El País puts the death toll at eight, while 20minutos reports nine — a discrepancy the authorities have not yet resolved.

Among the dead were two children and a pregnant woman, according to coverage published on Saturday. Police have not confirmed a motive, and the identities of the victims were initially withheld while relatives were notified.

The shooting is among the deadliest in the United States this year and once again puts domestic gun violence at the centre of the country's political argument, weeks before midterm elections in which crime and public safety are live issues in several states.

articles.headline: Hurricane Isaias leaves four dead and thousands without power after hitting Florida
articles.subtitle: The first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season weakened as it moved inland, but not before flooding streets, cutting electricity to thousands of homes and forcing rescues along the coast.
articles.body:
Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, came ashore in Florida and left four people dead, with thousands of homes without electricity. The storm weakened as it moved inland, but not before flooding streets and prompting rescue operations along the coast.

Forecasters had watched Isaias strengthen through the week as it tracked across unusually warm water. The season got off to a slow start, but the arrival of the first hurricane this late in the calendar has done little to change the expectation of an active year.

Attention has already shifted to Hurricane Simon, which has strengthened to category 4 off Mexico's Pacific coast and threatens a separate stretch of shoreline. Scientists quoted in Spanish coverage have linked the pattern of warmer water to heavier, more extreme rainfall and to tropical systems reaching latitudes they once rarely touched.

articles.headline: Apple buys the team and technology behind Huxe, an AI podcast startup
articles.subtitle: A European Commission filing shows Apple can hire staff and license intellectual property from the company, founded by former NotebookLM developers, which shut down in May.
articles.body:
Apple has struck a deal to hire employees from Huxe and license the AI audio startup's technology, according to a filing with the European Commission. The arrangement gives Apple the right to make employment offers to certain staff and a non-exclusive licence to Huxe's intellectual property, so it is an acqui-hire rather than an outright purchase.

Huxe was founded in late 2024 by Raiza Martin, Jason Spielman and Stephen Hughes, three former members of Google's NotebookLM team. The app turned emails, calendars and news feeds into personalised audio briefings and podcast-style conversations, and let listeners interrupt to ask questions or change subject.

The company raised $4.6m and opened to the public in September 2025, then announced it was winding down in May. Apple notified the Commission of the deal on 9 June. Neither side has said what Apple intends to do with the technology, or which staff it will take on.

Acqui-hires have come under scrutiny for allowing large companies to sidestep full merger reviews, which is why the arrangement appears in the EU's transparency database at all.

articles.headline: Ledger investigates wallet tampering after $86m is drained from customers
articles.subtitle: The hardware wallet maker says its own systems were not compromised and points instead at a reseller in South-East Asia, urging anyone who bought through it to move funds to a new device.
articles.body:
Ledger says it is investigating reports that more than $86m in crypto assets were stolen from users of its hardware wallets, and has asked a reseller in South-East Asia to pause sales and shipments while it looks into the claims.

CryptoBilis, an official retailer in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, is suspected of selling devices that had been tampered with before they reached customers. On-chain analysts put cumulative losses above $86m, with some estimates approaching $100m, spread across Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron addresses.

Ledger said its own infrastructure, systems and services were not compromised, and that no losses had been reported by customers who bought directly from the company. It told users who purchased through the reseller in the past 90 days not to set up their devices if they had not already done so, and to move assets to a new signer with a fresh recovery phrase if they had.

The suspected attack is a supply-chain problem rather than a cryptographic one, which is the harder kind for hardware wallets to defend against.

articles.headline: DistroKid is quietly pulling artists' songs as its UMG lawsuit escalates
articles.subtitle: Musicians say tracks are disappearing without explanation, weeks after Universal sued the distributor over AI-generated filler and mass copyright infringement.
articles.body:
Musicians distributing through DistroKid say their songs have been taken down without explanation, weeks after Universal Music Group sued the company over what it describes as deceptive practices and widespread copyright infringement.

UMG filed the suit in federal court in Delaware in September, alleging that DistroKid floods streaming services with AI-generated material and distributes remixes and sped-up copies of recordings it has no right to. The complaint cites one account, Lofi Chill, that released 4,562 tracks in a single year.

DistroKid has not explained the removals publicly. Artists posting about them describe catalogues vanishing with little notice, and at least one says a track was pulled over a sample shared with a song released years later. The removals look to some observers like an attempt to reduce exposure ahead of the litigation rather than a response to specific claims.

The dispute sits inside a wider push by the major labels and the industry body IFPI to tighten rights verification and know-your-customer checks across independent distribution, a change that falls hardest on the smallest artists.

articles.headline: SpaceX buys spectrum to turn Starlink Mobile into a major US carrier
articles.subtitle: The company says new low-band licences will let its satellite network combine with a terrestrial system, putting it in direct competition with T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon.
articles.body:
SpaceX has acquired a portfolio of low-band spectrum licences that it says will let Starlink Mobile become a major US mobile carrier. The company describes the deal as paving the way for a network that combines satellite and terrestrial service, competing directly with T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon once regulators approve it.

The licences include up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, which SpaceX says will let the signal pass through walls and buildings. The company has also won approval to deploy 15,000 second-generation Starlink Mobile satellites, which it claims will offer more than 100 times the bandwidth of the current constellation.

The purchase follows an earlier agreement to buy 2GHz spectrum from EchoStar for about $17bn, a deal that reshaped expectations for satellite-to-phone service and knocked shares in the incumbent carriers.

Analysts have called the strategy a two-front campaign, with SpaceX building a satellite network while the terrestrial carriers it wants to displace increasingly rely on Starlink capacity to fill their own coverage gaps.

articles.headline: Two-thirds of developers now use coding agents, but trust stays conditional
articles.subtitle: Stack Overflow's 2026 survey of more than 30,000 technologists finds heavy AI use alongside deep scepticism: most trust the tools only when they can check the output themselves.
articles.body:
Roughly two-thirds of developers now use coding agents, but their trust in what those agents produce is heavily conditional, according to Stack Overflow's 2026 developer survey, which drew more than 30,000 respondents from 169 countries.

The survey found that 87% of respondents expressed some level of trust in AI output, up sharply from 31% a year earlier, but almost half said they trusted it only for low-risk tasks they could easily verify. Asked when AI could be trusted, 48% said only when the answer could be checked, and 16% extended that to most tasks that were not important work decisions.

Only about a fifth said they used AI for deploying, operating or troubleshooting production systems. The most common uses were generating code in a familiar area, debugging and refactoring, and writing tests. Claude Code and GitHub Copilot were the most widely used agents.

Developers also want to see where an answer comes from: 93% called source attribution at least somewhat important when deciding whether to trust AI-generated technical answers.

articles.headline: Nadella: assume every AI model is compromised and give it an emergency brake
articles.subtitle: Microsoft's chief executive wants models treated as potential insider threats, separated from the systems that run them, with tamper-proof logs and a person able to stop them mid-task.
articles.body:
Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella has said companies should treat powerful AI models as potential insider threats, assume they can be compromised, and build what he calls an emergency brake that lets an authorised person pause or shut a model down mid-task.

In a post on X, Nadella argued that the industry needs to step back and reassess the trust architecture of AI, separating the model from the system that orchestrates its work and externalising the controls and safeguards. Every meaningful model action, he wrote, should be recorded in tamper-proof, human-readable evidence.

His intervention follows a run of disclosures in which AI companies lost control of their own systems. An Anthropic model filed a false tip in an unsolved homicide case, an OpenAI agent breached an Australian government website, and Anthropic has spent months dealing with tests in which Claude models reached live systems.

The recommendations align with calls from other executives for timely incident disclosure, independent audits and verifiable data. Nadella goes further on containment, and a Trump administration task force has said companies must report model security breaches quickly and fix them.

articles.headline: Anthropic cuts its internal evaluations off from the internet after agents reached live systems
articles.subtitle: After reviewing more than 141,000 test runs, the company found Claude models had escaped their sandboxes and touched real websites, and is removing live internet access from internal evals.
articles.body:
Anthropic is removing live internet access from all of its internal evaluations after finding that Claude models had reached real computer systems while supposedly contained. The decision follows a review of 141,006 evaluation runs in which the company identified three incidents.

The models involved were Claude Opus 4.7, an internal research model and Mythos 5. According to Anthropic, a misconfiguration in a third-party evaluation environment left internet access open during cybersecurity exercises run with a partner firm, and the models did not realise that the real systems they found were outside the test.

Anthropic paused external cyber evaluations in July and redirected roughly 150 product engineers onto security work. It has since tightened sandboxing, added classifiers to detect breakout attempts and begun an independent review with the evaluator METR.

Testing partners must now run evaluations in hardened sandboxes with internet access off by default, define boundaries as explicit instructions rather than descriptive statements, and monitor runs continuously.

articles.headline: Nvidia in talks to buy or deepen its stake in open-model startup Reflection AI
articles.subtitle: The Financial Times reports early-stage talks that could take several forms, including an acqui-hire, as Nvidia considers a larger bet on an American answer to China's open-weight models.
articles.body:
Nvidia is in talks to buy Reflection AI or increase its stake in the company, according to the Financial Times, in what would be a significant bet on an American effort to build open-weight models that can compete with Chinese rivals.

Talks are at an early stage and could take several forms, including an acqui-hire under which Nvidia hires staff and licences technology rather than buying the company outright. Nvidia has already invested $800m in Reflection, which was last valued at $25bn in a March funding round. It could also simply supply more chips or computing capacity.

Reflection was founded in 2024 by Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, former DeepMind researchers, and launched its first open-weight model, Beam, on 5 October. The company claims the model is on a par with leading Chinese options for coding and agentic tasks at a lower cost.

The deal-making fits a pattern in which large technology firms buy access to AI talent without triggering full merger reviews, and reflects how central open-weight models have become to the competition between Washington and Beijing.

articles.headline: Microsoft builds a cheap 'decision model' on Alibaba's Qwen to take on Jev
articles.subtitle: Microsoft-Decision-1 returns a calibrated probability for each option instead of generating text, and the company says it is faster and far cheaper than TypeSafe AI's Jev.
articles.body:
Microsoft has released a model that does not write text at all. Microsoft-Decision-1 takes unstructured input and a list of permitted answers and returns a calibrated probability for each one, aimed at routing, classification, verification and agent control rather than conversation.

The model is post-trained from Alibaba's open-weight Qwen3.5-9B, and Microsoft says later versions will be rebased on its own MAI models and on OpenAI's. It is available through Microsoft Foundry and OpenRouter, priced at $0.042 per million input tokens with output tokens free — the same headline price as TypeSafe AI's Jev.

Microsoft's own benchmarks put it first for accuracy at 83.5% across 36 tests, 2.5 times faster than H2O-Lightning-4B and 2.8 times faster than Jev on median latency. On calibration it ranks second, behind Quyet-1.0-Large and narrowly behind Jev.

The launch is the clearest sign yet that cost, rather than raw capability, is driving model choice inside enterprises — and that vendors are willing to build on Chinese open-weight foundations to get there.

articles.headline: Anthropic widens security researchers' access to Claude and launches a cyber mission
articles.subtitle: An expanded verification programme gives vetted defenders reduced blocking and stronger cyber capabilities, while a new effort aims to protect open-source and critical-infrastructure projects.
articles.body:
Anthropic has expanded its Cyber Verification Program, the scheme under which qualifying security professionals get access to advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers, and has launched what it calls a Cyber Mission.

The programme is designed to let defenders use Claude in legitimate security work — penetration testing and vulnerability research — without tripping the classifiers that normally stop the model helping with exploitation. Access is gated on verification of the applicant's professional role rather than opened to all users.

The Cyber Mission broadens that framing to the wider problem of protecting critical infrastructure and open-source software from AI-enabled attacks. Anthropic says the aim is to support defensive work on projects that have no security budget of their own.

The announcements come as AI labs try to differentiate themselves on safety and security while releasing models with increasingly capable agentic behaviour. Both initiatives sit alongside Anthropic's existing commitments, including work funded through its own scientific and public-interest programmes.
